Diagnosis requires positive darkfield microscopy or a positive venereal disease research laboratory (VDRL) test or rapid plasma reagin (RPR) followed by confirmatory fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test or microhemagglutination-treponema pallidum (MHA-TP). C
The treatment of choice in adults with primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis is penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM in a single dose.B

background.definition: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by the organism treponema pallidum.

list.listitem: A total of 35.3 total cases of primary or secondary syphilis per 100,000 US adults were reported to health departments in 2018.
Rate of congenital syphilis was 33.1 per 100,000 live births in 2018.
The case rate of primary, secondary, and congenital syphilis has increased significantly since 2014.

From 2017 to 2018, the incidence of syphilis increased significantly (13.3%). More than 85 percent of primary and secondary syphilis occurs in men, and 53 percent of male cases occur in men who have sex with men.
Syphilis is spread by direct contact with syphilis lesion, which most commonly appears on external genitalia, vagina, anus, or rectum, but is occasionally found on lips or mouth.
There is vertical transmission from mother to fetus.
The rash of secondary syphilis contains spirochetes, so contact with the rash can result in disease transmission.
Organisms reproduce locally, and then spread to regional lymph nodes and throughout the body via the circulatory system. The incubation period is 3 weeks to 3 months.
Primary syphilis: Chancre (ulcerated, nontender lesion) heals without treatment in 2 weeks to 8 weeks.
Secondary syphilis results from spirochetemia and occurs after the primary lesion heals. Skin rash and mucous membrane lesions occur.

Late and latent stages may occur decades after untreated primary disease; the host immune response does not affect the organism. Latent syphilis is defined as seroreactivity without other evidence of disease. If seroconversion with more than a fourfold increase in nontreponemal titers, unequivocal symptoms of primary or secondary syphilis, or sex with a partner documented to have disease, has occurred within the past year, it is defined as early latent syphilis. After 1 year, any of these criteria result in a diagnosis of late latent syphilis.
Tertiary disease: One third of latent diseases become tertiary, with neurologic or cardiovascular lesions due to end arteritis.
Screening is recommended by the USPSTF for all pregnant women and for persons who are at increased risk for infection. A
Consistent condom use, expedited partner therapy, and enhanced patient referral reduce the risk of infection or reinfection.B
All sexual partners should be screened, and treated if necessary. Perform HIV testing on all patients who are diagnosed with any stage of syphilis. C

Screening is recommended by the USPSTF for all pregnant women and for persons who are at increased risk for infection (eg, prostitutes and those who exchange sex for drugs, men having sex with men, adults in correctional facilities). Syphilis screening is also recommended for those individuals at high risk, defined as those with previous syphilis infection, a sexual partner with syphilis infection, HIV infection, and individuals who have had more than four sex partners in the previous year. In a high-risk population of incarcerated women, one must screen 10 patients to detect 1 case of syphilis. The USPSTF recommends against screening of asymptomatic persons not at increased risk; one must screen 24,000 low-risk asymptomatic patients to detect 1 case of syphilis. A

Screening consists of 2 stages: a nontreponemal test (VDRL or RPR) followed by confirmatory treponemal test (fluorescent treponemal antibody FTA-ABS or TP-PA). This algorithm may be in flux, as many laboratories now start with the treponemal test.
In a large RCT, male circumcision reduced the risk of HIV and HSV-2 infection but did not reduce the incidence of syphilis.
Consistent condom use reduces the risk of acquiring syphilis.

Expedited partner therapy (ie, the patient delivers medication or a prescription for medication to their partner(s) without the need for a medical examination of the partner) and enhanced patient referral (the patient tells their sexual partners that they need to be treated, either with additional support to enhance outcomes) both are associated with a decrease in the risk of subsequent re-infection of STIs including syphilis.

In a randomized trial of adults over the age of 18 presenting for a rapid HIV test to sexually transmitted disease clinics, individualized patient-centered risk-reduction counseling (including a discussion of patient-specific HIV/STI risk behaviors and negotiation of achievable risk-reduction steps, including the provision of any necessary referrals, lubricant, and condoms) at the time of rapid HIV testing among adults 18 years and older did not significantly reduce the risk of subsequent sexually transmitted infections (STIs) over the subsequent 6 months (12.3% vs 11.1% for those only given information). B

Suspect syphilis in patients with a single painless ulcer (chancre), those with contact with an infected patient or with commercial sex workers, men who have sex with men, and adults in correctional facilities.

Diagnosis requires positive darkfield microscopy of lesion fluid or positive nontreponemal tests (VDRL or RPR) with confirmation by treponemal antibody test (FTA-ABS, TP-PA, chemiluminescence immunoassay, or TPHA).

Differential.Differential_Features: Rare in the United States, painless ulcers, no adenopathy, beefy red lesions, bleed easily

list.listitem: Patients with primary syphilis usually present with 1 or more painless, hard ulcers in the genital region. Patients often have risk factors including unprotected sex, and may also have local, nontender lymphadenopathy.

Patients with secondary syphilis may have diffuse maculopapular hyperpigmented lesions (3-10 mm), scaling on palms and soles, patchy baldness, and condyloma lata around anus. One may be able to obtain the organisms from these lesions for darkfield microscopy.
Late symptoms occur 10 to 30 years after initial infection and include atypical psychosis, paralytic dementia, aortic aneurysm, and cardiac valve regurgitation.

In a case series of 284 consecutive individuals with syphilis since 2000 in Paris, France, over 95% were men most of whom (83%) were having sex with men. Just over half were HIV positive. Most had primary (29%) or secondary syphilis (45%) and most presented with a genital chancre (77%) and a diffuse exanthem (86%).

Congenital syphilis in newborns: hepatosplenomegaly; jaundice; rhinitis; failure to thrive; saddle nose; early rash of small blisters on palms and soles, which may later become copper-colored; and nasal discharge.
Congenital syphilis in older infants and young children: abnormal notched teeth, bone pain, blindness, corneal clouding, decreased hearing, saber shins.

Darkfield microscopy of fluid obtained from ulcer may reveal spirochetes (lightly abrade the ulcer with gauze and collect serous exudate that emerges from the specimen). A negative darkfield microscopy examination does not rule out disease.
CDC 2021 guidelines recommend that all patients diagnosed with syphilis should also be tested for HIV disease.

Diagnostic testing for syphilis involves two stages, first with a non-treponemal test followed by a confirmatory treponemal test. Initial serologic nontreponemal tests are the RPR and VDRL test. Nontreponemal tests will not become positive until 3 to 4 weeks after the appearance of the chancre, so the initial RPR or VDRL may need to be repeated after 4 weeks, if initially negative. High titers of RPR are more specific for syphilis infection than low titers, which may occur in pregnancy and autoimmune disease.
If positive, a nontreponemal test must be confirmed by FTA-ABS or Microhemagglutination Assay for Treponema Pallidum (MHA-TP) The MHA-TP is the test of choice for verifying syphilis.

Latent stage syphilis: VDRL or RPR may be positive early, but this wanes with time. Make a diagnosis of latent syphilis when there is a fourfold increase in titer in serologic tests in a person with a history of syphilis. A suggestive diagnosis is based on a reactive VDRL or RPR and a history of exposure within the past year, or a previously negative VDRL titer.

Tertiary syphilis: Thirty percent of patients will have nonreactive VDRL or RPR, so when tertiary syphilis is suspected, obtain an FTA-ABS or MHA-TP, even when the nontreponemal tests are negative. Obtain a CSF VDRL if tertiary syphilis is suspected to rule out neurosyphilis.

Order an FTA-ABS when evaluating for neurosyphilis, as this test detects IgM. Diagnosis of neurosyphilis requires a positive serum FTA-ABS or MHA-TP a CSF cell count of more than 5 mononuclear cells per mL, and a CSF total protein of greater than 40 mg/dL. Definitive diagnosis requires a positive CSF VDRL.

All infants of mothers with positive serologic tests should be evaluated with RPR or VDRL on infant serum. If congenital syphilis is suspected, order a pathologic examination of placenta and cord with FTA staining.

Results of tests after treatment: Check titers of nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) at 3-month intervals for 1 year. After adequate treatment for primary and secondary syphilis, titers should decrease fourfold by the end of the third or fourth month after treatment and eightfold after 6 months to 8 months. In patients with latent or tertiary syphilis, titers may remain at 50% of previous levels for 2 years.
Treponemal tests may remain positive for life, despite adequate treatment for disease, so treponemal tests are not useful for measuring treatment efficacy.
Note that the FTA-ABS may be falsely positive in a patient with Lyme disease or systemic lupus erythematosus.
Consider syphilis in individuals who present with painless genital ulcers, especially if in individual is at high risk of syphilis or has a history of unprotected sex.
When primary or secondary syphilis is suspected order a nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL) and if positive (titer at least 8:1) confirm with the MHA-TP or the FTA-ABS.
Tertiary syphilis: Order FTA-ABS or MHA-TP, even when the nontreponemal tests are negative. Obtain a CSF VDRL in suspected cases of tertiary syphilis to rule out neurosyphilis.
A definitive diagnosis of neurosyphilis requires a positive CSF VDRL.
Suspected congenital syphilis: order an FTA-ABS to detect IgM.
Adult treatment for primary, secondary and early latent syphilis: penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million U IM in a single dose based on 2021 CDC guidelines. A
Adult treatment for late latent or tertiary syphilis with normal CSF: penicillin G procaine 2.4 million IU IM once weekly for 3 week. A

Neurosyphilis and ocular syphilis: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18 to 24 million units per day, administered as 3 to 4 million units IV every 4 hours or continuous infusion, for 10 to 14 days (2021 CDC guidelines). A
Based on 2021 CDC guidelines:
Primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis: The treatment of choice is penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units IM in a single dose.
Late latent syphilis: Penicillin G benzathine 7.2 million units total, administered as 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals.
Tertiary syphilis with normal CSF examination: Penicillin G benzathine 7.2 million units total, administered as 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals.

Neurosyphilis, otosyphilis and ocular syphilis: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18 to 24 million units per day, administered as 3 to 4 million units IV every 4 hours or continuous infusion, for 10 to 14 days. An alternative regimen that requires assurance of compliance is procaine penicillin 2.4 million units IM once daily plus probenecid 500 mg orally 4 times a day, both for 10 to 14 days.

A single dose of oral azithromycin 2 grams may be equivalent to an IM penicillin regimen for early primary syphilis. However, 2021 CDC guidelines caution against using azithromycin as first-line treatment due to emerging evidence of resistance. Another option is desensitization followed by benzathine penicillin.
Recommendations for patients with comorbid HIV are similar as for patients without HIV disease, although close follow-up after treatment to confirm cure is needed.
In a small case series of patients with optic nerve involvement in neurosyphilis, the addition of corticosteroids was found to be of benefit in restoring vision.

A meta-analysis identified 27 studies with 2710 participants comparing different antibiotics for treatment of non-neurological syphilis. They found that ceftriaxone, doxycycline and azithromycin were all similarly effective to penicillin.

In penicillin-allergic patients with primary or secondary syphilis, give doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days or tetracycline 500 mg 4 times daily for 14 days, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM daily for 8 to 10 days.
Treatment in pregnancy: Penicillin is effective in the treatment of syphilis in pregnancy and prevents congenital syphilis, but the optimal regimen has not yet been identified.

Management of contacts: Treat any individuals exposed to the patient within 90 days preceding the patient's diagnosis of primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis. Use the regimen for primary syphilis.
Treponemal tests should be performed 3, 6, 9, and 12 months after treatment for primary syphilis and should become negative.
The treatment of primary and secondary syphilis usually results in a cure. Data show that only 15% of patients with early syphilis will not achieve a serologic response at 1 year after treatment.
Untreated primary syphilis results in spirochetemia, which progresses to secondary and then latent syphilis if untreated. Not all patients manifest signs and symptoms of secondary syphilis.

In the controversial Tuskegee study, after 15 years of untreated infection, 75% of men had syphilitic complications of the cardiovascular system, central nervous system, and joints; this was 4 times the rate of these complications in uninfected control patients.
The mortality rate after 20 years was 40% in the untreated group, compared with 27% in the control group.

A prospective study in Oslo followed 1978 patients with primary or secondary syphilis that was not treated. Ultimately, 28% of patients developed complications of late disease, including cardiovascular syphilis (10%), neurosyphilis (6.5%), and late benign syphilis (16%), with men more frequently affected with all complications than women.
The treatment of primary and secondary syphilis usually results in a cure. Data show that only 15% of patients with early syphilis will not achieve a serologic response at 1 year after treatment.
Limited information is available concerning the clinical response and follow-up of patients who have tertiary syphilis.

Follow the nontreponemal antibody titers (VDRL or RPR) every 3 months for 1 year (2 years in patients infected with HIV). Titers should decrease fourfold by the end of 6 to 8 months, and eightfold at 1 year.
For latent and tertiary syphilis, follow the VDRL or RPR titers for 2 years. In some cases, these may not drop below 50% of the initial value until after 2 years.

If patients have persistent signs or symptoms, or have a sustained fourfold increase in a nontreponemal test titer, retreat them, as treatment may have failed, or they may be reinfected. Retreatment consists of weekly IM injections of penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units for 3 weeks.
There is no definitive test of cure for syphilis.

In a population-based study of cases of syphilis in British Columbia, Canada, 10% of new cases of syphilis in the province were attributed to individuals who had received a previous diagnosis of syphilis within the preceding 10 years.
Treatment of latent syphilis does not affect transmission.
There is no clear evidence regarding when a treated patient is no longer contagious. Individuals with secondary syphilis are contagious at least as long as the rash is present.

Treat HIV-positive patients who have syphilis with the same stage-specific treatments as non-HIV-infected patients. Some experts recommend using the extended regimen (as used for late syphilis) with a total of 7.2 million units of penicillin G benzathine for patients who are infected with HIV.

CSF pleocytosis is common in patients with HIV, so some experts recommend a CSF examination before treatment of any stage of syphilis in patients infected with HIV, followed by another CSF examination after treatment.
Note that patients infected with HIV may have unusually high nontreponemal titers, or their seroreactivity may be delayed.
Patients infected with HIV should have serologic and clinical evaluation for cure at 3, 6, 9, 12, and 24 months after therapy.
Screen all pregnant women for syphilis with VDRL, and confirm positive tests with FTA-ABS.

Treat pregnant women who are diagnosed with syphilis with penicillin. The best treatment regimen for pregnant women is unknown. The Centers for Disease Control recommends using the appropriate regimen for the stage of syphilis.
Some experts recommend ultrasound screening of infected women to look for signs of congenital syphilis (hepatomegaly, ascites, thickened placenta, or hydrops).

Follow-up: Repeat serologic titers at 28 to 32 weeks of gestation, at delivery, and following the recommendations for the stage of disease. Some experts recommend a second dose of penicillin G benzathine 2.4 million units 1 week after the first dose.

Treatment is likely to be inadequate if delivery occurs within 30 days of the first treatment of the mother, if clinical signs of infection are present at delivery, or if the maternal antibody titer is fourfold higher than the pretreatment titer.
Based 2021 CDC guidelines:

Congenital syphilis in infants with proven or highly probable disease: aqueous crystalline penicillin G 100,000–150,000 units/kg body weight/day, administered as 50,000 units/kg body weight/dose by IV every 12 hours during the first 7 days of life and every 8 hours thereafter for a total of 10 days.

Possible congenital syphilis: Aqueous crystalline penicillin G 100,000–150,000 units/kg body weight/day, administered as 50,000 units/kg body weight/dose by IV every 12 hours during the first 7 days of life and every 8 hours thereafter for a total of 10 days.
Early latent syphilis in children: benzathine penicillin 50,000 units/kg upt to the adult dose of 2.4 million units in a single IM dose.
Late latent syphilis in children: as for early latent syphilis but repeated twice, i.e. 3 doses given at 1 week intervals for a total of 150,000 units/kg up to a maximum dose of 7.2 million units.
